hero.title: The Complete Guide to AI Reporting Workflows with Claude + MCP
hero.excerpt: Automate data collection, analysis, and reporting with Claude AI and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) in a secure, scalable architecture.

intro.text: Manual reporting is slow, repetitive, and error-prone. By combining Claude AI's advanced reasoning capabilities with the ==Model Context Protocol (MCP)==, you can build a powerful reporting workflow that collects data, analyzes it, and generates actionable insights—automatically.

blocks.text: **Claude** is an advanced AI assistant from Anthropic that excels at understanding, analyzing, and generating human-like text.
**MCP (Model Context Protocol)** is an open protocol that allows AI models like Claude to securely connect with external tools, data sources, and systems in a standardized way.
Together, Claude + MCP enable AI to access real-world data, perform complex analysis, and deliver business-ready reports in a consistent, repeatable workflow.

sections.heading: Why Use Claude and MCP for Reporting?

items.title: Save Time
items.text: Automate data gathering and report generation.

items.title: Increase Accuracy
items.text: AI minimizes human error and ensures consistency.

items.title: Deeper Insights
items.text: Claude analyzes data and explains trends clearly.

items.title: Scalable
items.text: Easily handle more data sources and complex reporting needs.

blocks.text: The workflow connects your data sources to Claude through MCP, processes the data, and outputs a well-structured report.

steps.title: Define the Reporting Goal
steps.text: Identify what metrics and insights your report should include.

steps.title: Connect Data Sources via MCP
steps.text: Use MCP connectors to pull data from your databases, APIs, or SaaS tools.

steps.title: Send Data to Claude
steps.text: Pass the retrieved data and reporting instructions to Claude for analysis.

steps.title: Analyze and Generate Insights
steps.text: Claude processes the data, identifies trends, and writes natural-language insights.

blocks.label: PRO TIP
blocks.text: Use Claude prompts that clearly define:
A weekly sales report that used to take an analyst three hours now runs in under a minute.

blocks.code: Prompt: "Using the attached orders export, write a weekly sales summary. Include revenue vs last week, top 5 products, and one risk to watch."

blocks.text: We went from a Monday-morning scramble to a report waiting in the inbox before anyone logged in.

items: Give Claude the smallest dataset that answers the question - not the whole database.
Version your prompts alongside your code.
Always keep a human review step before a report is shared externally.
Log every run so you can trace how a number was produced.

blocks.title: Watch your data scope

Official reference servers, custom Node/Python server

seo.title: Speeding Up Your Shopify Store: A Practical Checklist | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: A field-tested checklist for improving Shopify load times, from image handling and app audits to theme code and Core Web Vitals.

hero.title: Speeding Up Your Shopify Store: A Practical Checklist
hero.excerpt: A field-tested checklist for improving Shopify load times, from image handling and app audits to theme code and Core Web Vitals.

intro.text: Speed is a conversion feature. A one-second delay on mobile can measurably drop add-to-cart rate. This is the checklist we run on every ==Shopify performance audit==, in the order we run it.

blocks.text: You cannot improve what you have not measured. Get a baseline on a **real device on 4G**, not just a desktop lab score.

items: Run PageSpeed Insights on the home page, a collection, and a product page.
Record Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).
Check the field data section - that is what Google actually ranks on.

blocks.title: Target numbers
blocks.text: LCP under 2.5s, INP under 200ms, CLS under 0.1 - measured on mobile field data, not lab.

sections.heading: Fix Images First - It Is Usually the Biggest Win

items.title: Serve modern formats
items.text: Shopify auto-serves WebP - make sure your theme uses the image_url filter, not hardcoded src.

items.title: Right-size
items.text: Never ship a 3000px hero to a 400px phone. Use responsive srcset with width descriptors.

items.title: Lazy-load below the fold
items.text: loading="lazy" on everything except the LCP image.

items.title: Reserve space
items.text: Always set width and height so the layout does not jump (CLS).

blocks.text: Every app can inject JavaScript into every page. The average store carries 3-6 apps it no longer uses.

rows: Keep if it earns its keep in revenue

blocks.title: Uninstalling is not enough
blocks.text: Many apps leave Liquid snippets and script tags behind. Search your theme for the app name after removing it.

steps.title: Defer non-critical JavaScript
steps.text: Add defer to script tags that are not needed for first paint.

steps.title: Preload the LCP image and fonts
steps.text: One rel=preload for the hero image and your primary web font.

steps.title: Remove unused CSS
steps.text: Old sections and settings often leave dead styles in theme.css.

steps.title: Cut render-blocking third parties
steps.text: Load chat widgets and analytics after the page is interactive.

blocks.text: Re-run the same three pages on the same device. Then add a monthly recurring check so regressions from new apps or campaigns get caught early.
We cut LCP from 4.1s to 2.0s on mobile and add-to-cart rate went up 9% the same month.

items.q: Does a higher PageSpeed score guarantee more sales?
items.a: No. It removes a barrier. Speed helps most when your store is currently slow on mobile; going from 90 to 95 rarely moves revenue.

items.q: Should I switch themes for speed?
items.a: Only if your current theme is an old vintage (non-OS 2.0) build. A modern theme plus this checklist usually beats a rushed migration.

items.q: Are page builders always slow?
items.a: Not always, but they add weight. Use them for landing pages, not your core product template.

seo.title: The Checkout Friction Audit: Find What Is Costing You Sales | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: A structured way to walk your own checkout, score every point of friction, and prioritise the fixes that recover the most revenue.

hero.title: The Checkout Friction Audit: Find What Is Costing You Sales
hero.excerpt: A structured way to walk your own checkout, score every point of friction, and prioritise the fixes that recover the most revenue.

intro.text: Most stores obsess over traffic and ignore the last 30 seconds of the journey. A ==checkout friction audit== is the cheapest CRO work you can do: no tools, no budget, just one focused hour walking your own funnel like a first-time buyer.

blocks.text: Friction compounds. A tiny hesitation at each step adds up to a closed tab. Write down every screen between product and confirmation.

sections.heading: Walk It on a Phone, on Data

steps.title: Use a real phone on cellular
steps.text: Not desktop, not wifi. Most abandonment happens on mobile data.

steps.title: Buy something for real
steps.text: Go all the way to a completed order. Refund it after.

steps.title: Narrate out loud
steps.text: Every time you pause, squint, or reach for information you do not have - that is friction. Note it.

steps.title: Repeat as a guest
steps.text: No saved address, no autofill. That is your hardest-working new customer.

blocks.text: If you hesitate for even half a second, a real customer hesitates longer - and some of them leave. Every pause is a line item.
Rate every issue you found on impact and effort, then sort. Fix high-impact / low-effort first.

rows: No express payment (Shop Pay / Apple Pay)
Surprise shipping cost at final step

sections.heading: The Fixes That Show Up Every Time

items.title: Enable express checkout
items.text: Shop Pay, Apple Pay, Google Pay above the fold in cart and checkout.

items.title: Show shipping early
items.text: Estimate cost and date in the cart, before the customer commits.

items.title: Guest checkout default
items.text: Offer an account after purchase, never before.

items.title: Trust near payment
items.text: Return policy, secure-payment note, and support contact by the pay button.

blocks.title: Do not fix everything at once
blocks.text: Ship changes in small batches so you can tell which one moved the number.
Track cart-to-checkout and checkout-to-purchase rates weekly. A friction audit that does not change those numbers was a list, not a fix.
Removing forced signup and adding Shop Pay took an afternoon and lifted checkout completion by 11%.

items.q: How often should I run this?
items.a: Once a quarter, and always after a theme update, a new checkout app, or a payment provider change.

items.q: Shopify checkout is locked down - what can I actually change?
items.a: Plenty: express payments, cart page UX, shipping presentation, trust content, and (on Plus) checkout extensions.

items.q: Do I need session recording tools?
items.a: They help, but the manual walk-through finds most issues for free. Add tools once you have exhausted the obvious.

seo.title: Reading A/B Test Results Without Fooling Yourself | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: The statistical traps that make losing tests look like winners, and a simple discipline for calling results you can trust.

hero.title: Reading A/B Test Results Without Fooling Yourself
hero.excerpt: The statistical traps that make losing tests look like winners, and a simple discipline for calling results you can trust.

intro.text: The hardest part of A/B testing is not running the test - it is not lying to yourself about the result. ==Peeking, tiny samples, and ignored guardrail metrics== turn noise into false confidence, and false confidence ships changes that quietly cost money.

sections.heading: "95% Significant" Is Not a Finish Line

blocks.text: Statistical significance tells you the result is unlikely to be pure chance *given the data so far*. It says nothing about whether you collected enough data, or whether you looked too early.

blocks.title: Peeking inflates false positives
blocks.text: If you check the dashboard daily and stop the moment it hits 95%, your real false-positive rate is closer to 25-30%, not 5%.

sections.heading: Decide the Rules Before You Launch

items: Pick the primary metric. One. Everything else is a guardrail or secondary.
Estimate the minimum detectable effect you would care about.
Use a sample-size calculator to get the required visitors per variant.
Convert that to a duration in whole business weeks, and commit to it.

blocks.label: PRO TIP
blocks.text: Write these four numbers in the test ticket before it goes live:
A variant can lift clicks and wreck revenue. Always read the whole picture.

rows: New friction later in the funnel
Segment before you roll out to everyone

blocks.text: A 50/50 test that delivered 54/46 has a **sample ratio mismatch**. Something is broken - a redirect, a bot filter, an analytics gap - and the result is not trustworthy, however pretty the graph.

blocks.title: Quick gut check
blocks.text: With tens of thousands of visitors, a genuine 50/50 split stays within roughly a percentage point. Bigger gaps need investigation, not interpretation.

items.title: Ship it
items.text: Hit the pre-planned sample, significant on primary, guardrails clean.

items.title: Re-run it
items.text: Promising but under-powered, or a data issue mid-flight.

items.title: Kill it
items.text: Flat or negative at full sample. A clean null is a real, useful result.

items.title: Segment then decide
items.text: Strong on one device or audience, neutral elsewhere.

blocks.text: Half our "winners" stopped winning once we forced ourselves to wait for the planned sample size.

items.q: Can I ever stop a test early?
items.a: Only to stop a clearly harmful variant, or if the tool uses a sequential/Bayesian method designed for continuous monitoring. Not to lock in a win.

items.q: What if the test never reaches significance?
items.a: That is an answer: the effect is smaller than you hoped. Ship the cheaper variant or move on.

items.q: How many tests should be winners?
items.a: Industry-wide, roughly 1 in 5 to 1 in 8. If most of your tests win, your analysis is too loose.

seo.title: Building a Pre-Launch QA Process That Scales | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: How to turn ad-hoc launch-day panic into a repeatable QA process: environments, a tiered checklist, automation, and a go/no-go gate.

hero.title: Building a Pre-Launch QA Process That Scales
hero.excerpt: How to turn ad-hoc launch-day panic into a repeatable QA process: environments, a tiered checklist, automation, and a go/no-go gate.

intro.text: Every store has a QA process. For most it is called "the founder clicks around for ten minutes and hopes." That works until it does not - usually on the highest-traffic day of the year. A ==repeatable QA process== is boring on purpose, and it scales with your release cadence.

sections.heading: Test Somewhere That Looks Like Production

blocks.text: Bugs hide in the gap between your test setup and the real store. Close that gap first.

items: Use a duplicate theme or a dedicated staging store, not the live theme's edit mode.
Seed realistic data: real product counts, real collection sizes, a discount code, an out-of-stock variant.
Test with production-like apps installed - app conflicts are a top launch-day failure.

blocks.title: Keep a throwaway order path
blocks.text: A $0.01 hidden product plus a 100%-off code lets you complete real checkouts without touching payouts.

sections.heading: A Checklist With Tiers, Not 200 Flat Items

blocks.text: Nobody runs a 200-line checklist honestly. Split it by risk so the right depth matches the change.

items.title: Smoke (every deploy)
items.text: Home, collection, product, cart, checkout complete. 5 minutes.

items.title: Core (weekly release)
items.text: Search, filters, account, discounts, email receipts, key landing pages.

items.title: Cross-device (theme change)
items.text: iOS Safari, Android Chrome, one small viewport, one desktop.

items.title: Full regression (big launch)
items.text: Everything, plus load test and analytics/pixel verification.

steps.title: Pick the tier
steps.text: Match it to the size of the change, decided by the person merging.

steps.title: Run it on staging
steps.text: Log every failure with a screenshot, URL, device, and steps to reproduce.

steps.title: Triage
steps.text: Blocker, major, or minor. Blockers stop the release; minors get tickets.

steps.title: Re-test fixes only
steps.text: Verify each fix and one thing around it - not the whole checklist again.

blocks.label: PRO TIP
blocks.text: A good bug report has all of these - missing one wastes a round-trip:
You will never automate everything, and you should not try. Automate the checks that are identical every time and expensive to miss.

rows: Highest cost of failure, stable steps
Visual layout of a campaign page
Changes constantly, human eye is faster
Silent when broken, big blind spot

blocks.text: One named person makes the call, against written criteria, and records it. That is the whole ritual - it just has to happen every time.

blocks.title: Ship criteria
blocks.text: Zero open blockers, smoke suite green on staging and production, rollback plan written, owner on call for two hours after launch.

blocks.alt: A team reviewing a launch checklist on a screen
blocks.caption: The gate is a five-minute conversation, not a committee.

items.q: We are a team of two. Is this overkill?
items.a: Scale it down: just the smoke tier and a one-line go/no-go. The structure matters more than the size.

items.q: What should we automate first?
items.a: The checkout-complete path. It has the highest cost of failure and the most stable steps.

items.q: How do we stop the checklist rotting?
items.a: Review it after every incident. If a bug reached production, add or change one line so it cannot happen silently again.

seo.title: Designing Product Pages That Sell | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: A design-led breakdown of the product page: hierarchy, imagery, the buy box, proof, and the details that quietly decide the sale.

hero.title: Designing Product Pages That Sell
hero.excerpt: A design-led breakdown of the product page: hierarchy, imagery, the buy box, proof, and the details that quietly decide the sale.

intro.text: The product page is where browsing becomes buying. Good PDP design is not decoration - it is ==answering the customer's questions in the order they ask them==, and removing every reason to hesitate before the add-to-cart tap.

blocks.text: On mobile the customer sees one screen at a time. Decide what each screen has to accomplish before you choose a single colour or font.
If a first-time visitor cannot tell what the product is, what it costs, and how to buy it within one thumb-scroll, the design has failed - regardless of how it looks.

items.title: Show scale
items.text: The product in a hand, on a body, in a room. Absolute size is invisible without context.

items.title: Show the range
items.text: Every colourway and key angle. Missing an angle reads as hiding something.

items.title: Show detail
items.text: One tight crop of texture, stitching, or finish quality.

items.title: Design for the phone
items.text: First image must read at 375px wide. Test it there, not on your monitor.

sections.heading: The Buy Box Is Sacred Space

blocks.text: Price, variant selection, quantity, and the add-to-cart button. Nothing competes with these. Every extra element here is a tax on the conversion.

items: Selected variant is always obvious - a state, not a guess.
Unavailable combinations are visibly disabled, not silently broken.
The button says what happens next ("Add to cart"), never just "Submit".
Shipping estimate and return terms sit one line below, not three taps away.

blocks.title: Sticky bars help - until they cover content
blocks.text: A sticky add-to-cart on mobile lifts conversion, but make sure it never hides the variant picker or size guide.

steps.title: Rating near the title
steps.text: A star rating by the product name answers "is this any good?" instantly.

steps.title: Reviews after the description
steps.text: Once they know what it is, they want to know if it delivered.

steps.title: Photos from customers
steps.text: Real-world images beat studio shots for believability.

steps.title: Objection-handling FAQ last
steps.text: Fit, care, compatibility, delivery - the questions that stall a purchase.

blocks.text: We moved the review stars up next to the title and nothing else. PDP conversion rose about 6%.

sections.heading: The Details That Quietly Decide It

rows: Size guide in a modal, not a new page
Keeps the customer in the flow
Fake urgency is detected and punished

blocks.title: The test
blocks.text: Read your PDP as someone about to spend their own money on a brand they have never heard of. Every unanswered question is a lost sale.

items.q: How long should the description be?
items.a: Short value copy high up, full detail lower down. Let confident buyers add to cart in seconds and researchers keep scrolling.

items.q: Video or photos?
items.a: Photos are non-negotiable. Video is a strong addition for products where motion, fit, or use is hard to convey in a still.

items.q: Should every product page look identical?
items.a: The structure should. The content depth can flex - a $15 accessory needs far less page than a $400 mattress.

seo.title: Shopify Canvas Explained: Shopify's AI Store Builder | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: Shopify Canvas lets you build and redesign a Shopify store by chatting with Sidekick. How it works, what it costs, what it can't do yet, and who should try it.

hero.title: Shopify Canvas: Build Your Store by Chatting With AI
hero.excerpt: Shopify Canvas lets you build and redesign a Shopify store by chatting with Sidekick. How it works, what it costs, what it can't do yet, and who should try it.

intro.text: Shopify launched ==Shopify Canvas== on October 1, 2026, and it changes how you build a store. Instead of dragging sections around the theme editor, you chat with **Sidekick**, Shopify's AI agent, and watch your store rebuild itself live.
We've been testing it on our own store. Here's what Shopify Canvas is, how it works, what it costs, what it can't do yet, and whether you should use it for your store today.

blocks.text: Shopify Canvas is a new AI design workspace inside Shopify Admin. It puts every template of your store (home, product, collection and cart) side by side on one big board. You describe what you want to **Sidekick** in plain language, and it builds or redesigns the theme for you.
It isn't a separate website builder or a new theme. It's a new way to edit a Shopify theme, built into the admin you already use.
In short: Shopify Canvas is an AI store builder where a chat prompt is the starting point and the result is real Shopify theme code.

sections.heading: How It Works: Three Steps, No Code

steps.title: Describe it
steps.text: Tell Sidekick what you want in plain language, for example "Make my homepage feel bold and minimal".

steps.title: Watch it update
steps.text: Changes appear across your whole store as they happen. Zoom and pan the board to inspect each template.

steps.title: Fine-tune by hand
steps.text: Click any element to edit it manually. You stay in control of the final design.

blocks.alt: Slide showing the three Shopify Canvas steps: describe it, watch it update, fine-tune by hand
blocks.caption: Three steps, no code: describe, watch, fine-tune.

sections.heading: Not a Mockup: Real Theme Code

blocks.text: Most AI website builders show you a static preview. Shopify Canvas renders the **actual code behind your store**, so animations, interactions and layouts behave like the live site.

To make this work, Shopify let Sidekick work directly with theme files and simplified its theme architecture. That matters for anyone who has watched an AI mockup fall apart once a developer tries to build it: what you see in Canvas is the theme.

items.title: ~20 minutes
items.text: To a fully custom store, according to Shopify's Director of Product, Ben Sehl.

items.title: 25M+ theme edits
items.text: Made by Sidekick in the first half of 2026, before Canvas existed.

items.title: $0 extra
items.text: Included with your Shopify plan. Usage limits vary by plan.

blocks.text: There's no separate price for Shopify Canvas. It runs on Sidekick, which is included with your Shopify plan.

sections.heading: Reality Check: What Canvas Can't Do Yet

blocks.text: Canvas is early. Before you move a live store onto it, know what isn't supported at launch:

items: **Third-party themes:** only Shopify-made themes and custom themes open in Canvas.
**App blocks and extensions:** Sidekick can't add or configure them yet.
**Markets, translations and rollouts:** promised over time, not available at launch.
**Theme updates and mobile:** Canvas is desktop-only, and Canvas-edited themes don't get automatic theme updates.

blocks.alt: Slide listing what Shopify Canvas can't do yet: third-party themes, app blocks, markets and translations, theme updates and mobile
blocks.caption: It's early. Not everything works yet.

blocks.title: Test on a copy first
blocks.text: Duplicating a theme into Canvas creates a copy you can edit only in Canvas. Experiment on that copy, not your live theme.

items.title: Good fit
items.text: New stores, simple storefronts, quick redesigns and design experiments on a duplicated theme.

items.title: Wait a bit
items.text: Stores that depend on third-party apps, multiple markets or translations.

blocks.text: Our take: Canvas is great for new stores and quick redesign experiments. If your store leans on apps or sells in several markets, give it a few weeks while Shopify adds support.

Shopify now joins Wix, Squarespace, Webflow and Framer in making a chat prompt the starting point for a storefront. The difference is that Canvas works on real Shopify theme code that a developer can keep building on.

Canvas makes it much faster to produce a new homepage or product page. It doesn't tell you whether that design sells more. A bold new layout can still lower conversion rate if it hides delivery information, reviews or the Add-to-Cart button.

blocks.label: PRO TIP
blocks.text: Before you publish a Canvas redesign:
checklist: QA it on real iPhones and Android phones, not just the desktop board
Check that tracking and pixels still fire
Run the new design as an A/B test against your current theme
Measure revenue per visitor, not just how it looks

blocks.text: Our [A/B testing services](/ab-testing) and [Shopify QA team](/quality-assurance) can test a Canvas design before it replaces your live theme. Read our [hands-on first look at Shopify Canvas](/blog/shopify-canvas-first-look) and our [Canvas vs theme editor comparison](/blog/shopify-canvas-vs-theme-editor) next.

items.q: What is Shopify Canvas?
items.a: Shopify Canvas is an AI design workspace in Shopify Admin, launched on October 1, 2026. You build or redesign your store by chatting with Sidekick, Shopify's AI agent, and see every template on one board.

items.q: How much does Shopify Canvas cost?
items.a: There's no separate price. Canvas runs on Sidekick, which is included with your Shopify plan. Usage limits vary by plan.

items.q: Does Shopify Canvas work with my theme?
items.a: Only Shopify-made themes and custom themes open in Canvas at launch. Third-party themes aren't supported yet.

items.q: Can I use Shopify Canvas on mobile?
items.a: Not yet. Canvas is desktop-only at launch.

items.q: Will Canvas change my live store?
items.a: Canvas works on a duplicated copy of your theme, so your live theme stays untouched until you publish.

cta.text: We'll QA it and A/B test it against your current theme before it goes live.

seo.title: Shopify Canvas First Look: Hands-On Walkthrough | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: A hands-on first look at Shopify Canvas from our own Shopify admin: the store board, theme settings, Sidekick prompt bar, the duplicate theme, and what's missing.

hero.title: Inside Shopify Canvas: A Hands-On First Look
hero.excerpt: A hands-on first look at Shopify Canvas from our own Shopify admin: the store board, theme settings, Sidekick prompt bar, the duplicate theme, and what's missing.

intro.text: We opened ==Shopify Canvas== in our own Shopify admin to see what it's really like. Canvas is Shopify's new AI design workspace, launched on October 1, 2026. Instead of opening one template at a time, you see your whole store on a single board and work on it with **Sidekick**, Shopify's AI agent.

This is a hands-on walkthrough of what you see when you open it, what we liked, and what's still missing. New to Canvas? Start with our [Shopify Canvas overview](/blog/shopify-canvas-ai-store-builder).

sections.heading: Your Whole Store on One Board

blocks.text: The first thing you notice is the board. Home page, Products, Collections, Cart and All collections sit side by side. You pan around the board instead of opening one template at a time in the theme editor.

blocks.alt: Shopify Canvas board in the Shopify admin showing the product, collection and cart templates side by side
blocks.caption: Canvas in our own Shopify admin: every template on one board.

blocks.text: For design work, this is a big change. You can see how a change to the header or colour palette affects every page at once, instead of clicking through templates to check.

sections.heading: Design Controls Stay One Click Away

blocks.text: Theme settings live in a side panel, so you can adjust the look while the full store stays in view:

items: **Logo and favicon,** including a default and an inverse logo for transparent headers
**Colour palette** for the whole theme
**Typography,** including text colours

blocks.alt: Shopify Canvas theme settings panel with logo, favicon, colour palette and typography controls
blocks.caption: Theme settings in a side panel next to the board.

blocks.title: Real code, not a mockup
blocks.text: Canvas renders the actual theme code behind your store, not a static preview, so what you see is how the live store will behave.

sections.heading: Navigate Fast and Ask Sidekick Anytime

blocks.text: Around the board, the controls are simple:

items: **At the top:** a "Jump to" search, undo, redo, history and an Update button.
**At the bottom:** a "Work with Sidekick" prompt bar. This is where you describe changes in plain language.

blocks.alt: Shopify Canvas toolbar with Jump to search, undo, redo and Update, plus the Work with Sidekick prompt bar
blocks.caption: The toolbar at the top and the Sidekick prompt bar at the bottom.

blocks.text: There's no separate price for Canvas. It runs on Sidekick, which is included with your Shopify plan, with usage limits that vary by plan.

sections.heading: Spot the Detail: You're Working on a Copy

blocks.text: Look at the top left of the screen: our theme shows up as **"Copy of Horizon"**. Canvas opens a duplicate of your theme rather than your live one.

According to Shopify's coverage, that copy can only be edited in Canvas, and Canvas-edited themes don't get automatic theme updates. That's worth knowing before you commit to it for a long-term store design.

blocks.label: MY TIP
blocks.text: Keep your live theme safe while you experiment:
checklist: Keep your current live theme as a fallback
Note which apps and markets your store relies on before switching

sections.heading: What We Like and What's Missing

items.title: Liked
items.text: Seeing every template at once. A clean layout. Chat and manual editing in the same place.

items.title: Not yet
items.text: Third-party themes, app blocks and extensions, markets and translations aren't supported at launch.

items.title: Heads-up
items.text: Desktop only, and still early access.

blocks.text: If Canvas isn't in your admin yet, it's rolling out gradually to existing stores.

sections.heading: Before You Publish a Canvas Design

blocks.text: Canvas makes design changes fast, which makes testing more important, not less. A new layout built in minutes should still be checked on real devices and compared against your current design with real shoppers.

Our [Shopify development team](/shopify-development) can review a Canvas-built theme, and our [A/B testing services](/ab-testing) can test it against your live store before you switch. To decide whether Canvas or the classic editor suits your store, read [Shopify Canvas vs the theme editor](/blog/shopify-canvas-vs-theme-editor).

items.q: Where do I find Shopify Canvas?
items.a: Canvas opens from the Themes page in Shopify Admin. It's rolling out gradually, so it may not be in every admin yet.

items.q: Does Canvas edit my live theme?
items.a: No. Canvas works on a duplicate of your theme, shown as "Copy of" your theme name, so your live theme stays untouched.

items.q: What can I change in Canvas theme settings?
items.a: Logo and favicon, the colour palette and typography, in a side panel next to the store board. You can also ask Sidekick for changes in plain language.

items.q: Is Shopify Canvas free?
items.a: There's no separate price. Canvas runs on Sidekick, which is included with your Shopify plan, with usage limits that vary by plan.

cta.heading: Want a second opinion on a Canvas design?
cta.text: We'll review it, QA it on real devices and test it against your current theme.

hero.excerpt: Shopify Canvas vs the theme editor compared: editing, preview, theme support, app blocks, markets and updates, plus how to choose the right one for your store.

intro.text: Shopify's new ==Shopify Canvas== (launched October 1, 2026) lets you build and edit your store by chatting with **Sidekick**, its AI agent. But it doesn't replace the theme editor you already know.

Here's an honest side-by-side of Shopify Canvas vs the theme editor: how you edit, what you see, what each one supports, and which to use for your store. For the basics, see our [Shopify Canvas overview](/blog/shopify-canvas-ai-store-builder).

sections.heading: Round 1: Drag and Drop vs Just Ask

items.title: Theme editor
items.text: Pick a theme, then rearrange modular sections and blocks. You make every change yourself.

items.title: Canvas
items.text: Chat with Sidekick and describe what you want. You can still click any element to edit it by hand.

blocks.title: Same store. Different way to build it.
blocks.text: Canvas changes the editing tool, not your theme.

sections.heading: Round 2: One Page at a Time vs the Whole Store

blocks.text: The theme editor shows one template at a time. Canvas puts your templates side by side on one board (home, product, collection and cart) and renders the real theme code, not a static preview.

For store-wide changes, such as a new colour palette or header, seeing every page at once saves a lot of clicking. For detailed work on one template, the theme editor's focused view is still comfortable. See our [hands-on first look at Canvas](/blog/shopify-canvas-first-look) for screenshots of the board.

items: Third-party themes (only Shopify-made and custom themes open in Canvas)
App blocks and extensions
Markets and translations
Automatic theme updates for Canvas-edited themes

blocks.text: For many established stores, app blocks alone decide it. Reviews, subscriptions, upsells and many testing tools rely on app blocks or extensions, and Sidekick can't add or configure them in Canvas yet.

sections.heading: Round 4: Pick by Your Store, Not the Hype

items.title: Try Canvas if...
items.text: You're starting fresh, want fast design experiments, or run a simple storefront with a Shopify-made or custom theme.

items.title: Stay on the theme editor if...
items.text: You rely on third-party themes, app blocks and extensions, multiple markets or translations.

blocks.title: Good news: you don't have to choose
blocks.text: Canvas opens from the same Themes page as the theme editor. It works on a duplicated copy of your theme, so your live theme stays untouched. And Shopify says Canvas is an early product that won't replace the online store editor for now.

Use both. Try Canvas on a duplicated theme for fast design exploration, then decide what to keep based on data, not on how quickly it was built. Keep the theme editor for your live store while you depend on apps, markets or translations.

blocks.label: PRO TIP
blocks.text: A practical workflow for established stores:
checklist: Explore new layouts in Canvas on a theme copy
Rebuild the winning ideas as sections in your live theme
A/B test them against the current design before rolling out

blocks.text: Need help? Our [Shopify development team](/shopify-development) builds custom sections for Online Store 2.0 themes, and our [A/B testing services](/ab-testing) prove which design actually sells more.

items.q: Does Shopify Canvas replace the theme editor?
items.a: No. Shopify says Canvas is an early product that won't replace the online store editor for now. Both open from the same Themes page.

items.q: What's the main difference between Canvas and the theme editor?
items.a: In the theme editor you rearrange sections and blocks yourself, one page at a time. In Canvas you describe changes to Sidekick and see your whole store on one board, and you can still edit any element by hand.

items.q: Can I use app blocks in Shopify Canvas?
items.a: Not yet. App blocks and extensions aren't supported in Canvas at launch, so stores that depend on apps should stay on the theme editor for now.

items.q: Does Canvas work with third-party themes?
items.a: No. Only Shopify-made themes and custom themes open in Canvas at launch.

items.q: Which should I use for my store?
items.a: Try Canvas for new stores, simple storefronts and quick design experiments. Stay on the theme editor if you rely on third-party themes, app blocks, multiple markets or translations.
